title.official: Incorrect parties not fatal to actions

subdivision.heading: Joining and Separating Claims and Parties

operative_text.controlling:
3.73(1)  No claim or action fails solely because
(a) 2 or more parties join in an action that they should not
have joined,
(b) 2 or more parties do not join an action that they could or
should have joined, or
(c) a party was incorrectly named as a party or was
incorrectly omitted from being named as a party.
(2)  If subrule (1) applies, a judgment entered in respect of the
action is without prejudice to the rights of persons who were not
parties to the action.

BOOK_A.defined_terms: claim, judgment, party Lack of proper parties is usually a ground to add them, not a ground to refuse the substantive Joining an unsuitable co-plaintiff is no ground to dismiss the suit, and if the right one relief sought. is there, the wrong co-plaintiff should just be struck out and disregarded. If a suit is timely begun against a group of people who are not a separate legal person (such as a trade union) in the usual name of that group, the court can later substitute some members of that group as representative defendants, even if in the meantime the limitation period to sue expires.The lawsuit as originally framed is not a nullity, especially if the union defended on the merits and fully participated in discovery.The concept of nullity's proper range is very narrow, especially in light of the aims of modern Rules.Nullity should be used only in cases of prejudice or unfairness. Changing a defendant "John Doe"to the person's real name is not misnomer;it is correcting a pseudonym. Adding an additional defendant is not hard if the limitation period has not expired. But an additional plaintiff (or plaintiff by counterclaim) will not be added if it is completely clear that he or she has no arguable cause of action. Despite a motion to strike out part of a statement of claim a plaintiff can validly sue anyone for an actionable wrong, even if that person was working for someone else atthe relevant time.If an individual employee himself owed a duty of care to a customer, the customer could sue him for a breach of that duty.Such a suit is possible if the employee's conduct was itself a tort, or if his actions exhibited a separate identity or interest from that of the employer. Commentary on changing parties is found after R.3.74. 2Patterson v. commentary.text: Rule 3.73 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.73. In Charleston Estate v. RIC New Brunswick Inc., 2015 ABQB 306 (Master), Master Robertson said: 47 This Rule is differently worded than its predecessor, former Rule 40, which said, “Where it appears that an action is defective for want of parties, the Court may render judgment saving the rights of all persons not parties.” It may be that the current Rule, more detailed than its predecessor, was intended to have a more broad-reaching effect. …
